summary: The European Commission sent X a formal request for information under the Digital Services Act after warning that illegal content and disinformation about the Israel-Hamas war was circulating on the platform. The request could precede a formal investigation, but officials confirmed none has been opened yet. DSA breaches can bring fines of up to 6% of annual turnover, and X has deadlines of October 18 and October 31 to respond.
one_line: The EU sent X a formal DSA information request over Israel-Hamas war disinformation, a possible precursor to a formal investigation and fines up to 6% of turnover.
key_facts: The European Commission sent X a formal request for information late Thursday (October 12, 2023) under the Digital Services Act (DSA), a day after a public warning.
EU officials confirmed to TechCrunch that a formal investigation has not been opened at this point.
If opened, it would be the first DSA investigation since the compliance deadline for very large online platforms (VLOPs) kicked in this summer.
DSA non-compliance can trigger fines of up to 6% of annual turnover and potential blocking of a service for repeated infringements.
Elon Musk last projected X revenues of about $3 billion for the year, which would imply a fine of up to $180 million.

Thierry Breton, the EU's internal market commissioner, sent an 'urgent' letter to Musk citing 'indications' from 'qualified sources' that X was being used to spread illegal content and disinformation after Saturday's attacks.
X has until October 18 to provide information on 'the activation and functioning of X's crisis response protocol' and until October 31 to respond to the other requests.

The DSA's Article 36 'crisis response' mechanism lets the Commission adopt rapid measures on larger platforms in situations of 'serious threat', such as war; formal proceedings would be opened under Article 66.
X CEO Linda Yaccarino said 'tens of thousands' of pieces of content were removed, along with 'thousands' of posts and 'hundreds' of accounts linked to terrorist groups, violence or extremism.
Yaccarino said X had received no requests from Europol at the time; the article corrected an earlier error that said Interpol.
X reported more than 50 million posts globally over two days referencing the attack, and relies on its Community Notes feature as its main response to disinformation.
Musk pulled X out of the EU's Code of Practice on online disinformation earlier in 2023; Breton warned 'You can run but you can't hide.'
A September study commissioned via the Code of Practice suggested X is the worst of the major platforms for spreading disinformation.
TikTok and Meta have also been warned by the EU over Israel-Hamas war disinformation.
